How do you work out the time complexity of loops?

Nested loops multiply, sequential blocks add, and you drop constants and lower-order terms (O(3n² + 5n) is O(n²)). A loop variable that is multiplied or divided by a constant gives log n. Watch the geometric-series trap: an inner loop bounded by a doubling i sums to O(n) overall. Hidden costs count too: String += in a loop, list.remove(0) on an ArrayList and substring are each O(n).
How do you find the complexity of recursive code (recurrences and the Master theorem)?

Branching factor b and depth d give roughly O(b^d) calls, which is why backtracking over subsets is O(2ⁿ) and permutations O(n!). Memoisation changes the count to "number of distinct states × work per state", e.g. Fibonacci drops to O(n).
What is the space complexity of recursion?

Interviewers often catch candidates who say "O(1) space" for a recursive solution: each pending call is a stack frame. If depth can be large, convert to an iterative version with an explicit ArrayDeque, or use bottom-up DP. The output itself (e.g. the returned list) is usually not counted as auxiliary space, but say so explicitly.
What is amortized complexity? Give examples.

Amortized means the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence, not an average over random inputs. It is different from average-case analysis (e.g. HashMap O(1) average assumes a good hash spread). Use the "each element enters and leaves once" argument whenever a nested loop shares a pointer that only moves forward.
Big-O vs Big-Θ vs Big-Ω, and best/average/worst case

In interviews "Big-O" is used loosely to mean the tight worst-case bound, so state which case you mean: "O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst". Also state your variables clearly: a grid is O(R·C), a graph is O(V + E), string problems often depend on both length n and alphabet size k.
Why is HashMap O(1) "on average", and what is its worst case in Java?

Mention that a bad hashCode() (e.g. returning a constant) degrades performance, and that mutable keys break lookups. Choose TreeMap when you need ordering or range queries, and an int[26] array instead of a map for lowercase-letter counts, which is both faster and O(1) space.
How should you approach an unseen coding problem in the interview?

Think aloud the whole way: interviewers grade communication and reasoning, not just a correct final answer. Common optimisations: replace a nested search with a HashMap (O(n²) to O(n)), sort first to enable two pointers or binary search, precompute prefix sums, or cache repeated subproblems.
Brute force vs sort first vs HashSet: the three usual trade-offs (Contains Duplicate)

| Brute force (nested loops) | Sort, then scan neighbours | HashSet
Time | O(n²) | O(n log n) | O(n) average
Extra space | O(1) | O(1) to O(log n) for an int[] sort (more for objects) | O(n)
Changes the input | No | Yes (or copy it first) | No
Keeps original indices | Yes | No | Yes
When it wins | n is tiny | Memory is tight | Default choice
Interview tip: say all three out loud with their costs, then code the HashSet version. Mentioning the sort version shows you know how to trade memory for time.
ArrayList vs HashMap vs TreeMap vs PriorityQueue vs ArrayDeque: operation costs

Structure | Add | Remove | Lookup / contains | Ordered?
ArrayList | O(1) amortized at end | O(n) (shifts), O(1) at end | get(i) O(1), contains O(n) | Insertion order
HashMap / HashSet | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(1) average | No
TreeMap / TreeSet | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n), plus floor/ceiling | Sorted
PriorityQueue | O(log n) | poll O(log n), remove(x) O(n) | peek O(1), contains O(n) | Only the head
ArrayDeque | O(1) amortized at both ends | O(1) at both ends | contains O(n) | Insertion order
Rule of thumb: need "the smallest so far" → PriorityQueue; need "the closest key below x" → TreeMap; need "have I seen x" → HashSet. Picking the right structure is usually what turns O(n²) into O(n log n) or O(n).
O(n + m) vs O(n · m): when do two inputs multiply?

Code shape | Complexity | Example
Loop over A, then a separate loop over B | O(n + m) | Build a set from A, then check each item of B
Loop over B inside a loop over A | O(n · m) | Compare every pair; an n × m DP grid
Loop over A, binary search in sorted B | O(n log m) | Intersection with one sorted array
Graph BFS / DFS with adjacency list | O(V + E) | Each vertex and each edge handled once
Grid DFS | O(rows · cols) | Number of Islands
Interview tip: do not collapse two different inputs into one "n". Saying O(n · m) for an edit-distance grid, or O(V + E) for BFS, is more precise and interviewers notice it.
Recursion vs iteration: when should you rewrite a recursive solution as a loop?

| Recursion | Iteration (loop or explicit stack)
Readability | Natural for trees, backtracking, divide and conquer | Natural for arrays and linear scans
Extra space | O(depth) call-stack frames | O(1) for a loop; O(depth) on the heap for an explicit stack
Depth limit | Thread stack size; deep input throws StackOverflowError | Only heap memory
Tail-call optimisation in Java | Not done by the JVM | Not needed
Typical risk case | Linked list or skewed tree with 105 nodes | More code to manage the stack by hand
Rule of thumb: write the recursive version first if it is clearer. Switch to a loop or an explicit ArrayDeque when the depth can be O(n) on large input, such as a degenerate tree or a long linked list.
